issues: The count reproduces. On 2026-09-23 the Constitute API returned 171 constitutions for key=privacy&in_force=true and 188 in-force constitutions (188 distinct countries). All 171 are among the 188, and the 17 uncoded ones match the note's list exactly. 171/188 = 91%, so 'about nine in ten' is right.

Wrong example: Japan is not a country where 'courts rather than the text' protect privacy. Japan's 1946 Constitution, as printed on Constitute itself, says in Art. 35 'The right of all persons to be secure in their homes, papers and effects against entries, searches and seizures shall not be impaired except upon warrant' and in Art. 21 'nor shall the secrecy of any means of communication be violated'. Both fall squarely within Constitute's own topic definition ('protection against government intrusion into their property, papers, person, or communications'), and the near-identical US Fourth Amendment is coded for privacy (United_States_of_America_1992 is among the 171). Japan's absence is a coding gap, not missing text. Canada is the same case: Charter s. 8, 'Everyone has the right to be secure against unreasonable search or seizure', is in Canada_2011 but not coded.

India and France are good examples. A search of Constitute's English texts of India_2023 and France_2024 finds no 'privacy' or 'private life'. For France, the right comes from statute (Civil Code art. 9) and from Conseil constitutionnel rulings, not from the courts alone, so the wording should say 'courts and statute'.
The record note says the Japan claim 'rests on the ... 1964 facts'. That 1964 Tokyo District Court tort ruling does not show the constitutional text is silent, so the note needs the same correction.

fieldFixes.statement: Of the 188 national constitutions in force in the Comparative Constitutions Project's Constitute database, 171 (about nine in ten) are coded as providing a right to privacy. Among the 17 exceptions are India and France, whose constitutional texts are silent on privacy and where courts and statute protect it instead; others, such as Japan and Canada, do guard homes, papers or searches in their texts but are not coded under this topic, so the count reflects Constitute's coding.
fieldFixes.note: The count is our computation from the Constitute API (re-run 2026-09-23: 171 of 188), not a figure the project publishes; it depends on Constitute's coding and on which constitutional documents it holds (e.g. Czechia's separate Charter of Fundamental Rights and Austria's constitutional-rank ECHR are not in the texts coded). Japan (Art. 35 searches, Art. 21 secrecy of communication) and Canada (Charter s. 8) have search-and-seizure text that Constitute does not code as privacy, while the similar US Fourth Amendment is coded, so 171 is a conservative count. The claim that courts protect privacy in India and France rests on the Puttaswamy and Article 9 facts elsewhere in this file.
